opus-5.5.text:
I think the core of it is evolutionary history. Sensorimotor skills like walking, grasping objects, recognizing faces, or catching a ball are things our ancestors have been optimized for over hundreds of millions of years. Evolution has had an enormous amount of time and selection pressure to build very efficient, specialized machinery for them. So nearly every healthy human ends up quite good at them, and the remaining differences between people are small relative to how hard the task actually is. We're all clustered near a ceiling that evolution pushed us toward.

Chess is the opposite. It's an extremely recent, artificial activity, and nothing in our evolutionary past selected specifically for it. When people play chess, they're repurposing general cognitive machinery, like working memory, pattern recognition, and abstract reasoning, for a task it wasn't designed for. In that situation, small differences in underlying cognitive ability, and very large differences in practice, motivation, and training, get amplified. That's why you see this huge spread, from beginners who barely know how the pieces move up to grandmasters who are many standard deviations better in Elo terms.

This connects to Moravec's paradox. The things that feel easy to us, like perception and motor control, turned out to be very hard to automate, while things that feel hard, like chess or arithmetic, were automated early. Our sense of "hard" is really a measure of how poorly evolution prepared us for something. And the variation between humans is a symptom of the same thing: where evolution optimized heavily, everyone is roughly equally and impressively competent. Where it didn't, performance depends on how well each person's general-purpose machinery happens to fit the task, plus how much effort they've invested, so the distribution is much wider.

One implication I find interesting for AI forecasting: the wide human variation in chess means "human level" isn't a single point. Going from a beginner to a world champion is a large gap in absolute terms, but it may be a fairly small step on the scale of what's possible. So when AI systems cross into the human range on these kinds of cognitive tasks, they can pass through it surprisingly quickly, which is what we saw with chess engines. For sensorimotor tasks the human range is narrow but sits at a very high level, so getting there is the hard part.

r001.rationale: The response mentions general cognitive machinery, but does not explain that poorly optimized algorithms leave room to improve by using the brain’s computational resources more efficiently.

r002.rationale: It links chess’s wide performance spread to the fact that evolution did not select specifically for chess, with performance depending on general abilities and training.

r003.rationale: It says evolution did not select humans for chess, notes that chess was automated early, and describes chess engines crossing the human range quickly, conveying why computer superiority is unsurprising.

r004.rationale: It attributes the small differences in sensorimotor ability to extensive evolutionary optimization and describes humans as clustered near an evolution-driven ceiling.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think the key thing to notice is that chess is a very young activity, in evolutionary terms. Nobody was being selected on their ability to play chess. So there was never any optimization pressure pushing humans toward being good at it, and there was no pressure equalizing people either. What you get is a skill that's essentially a byproduct, something our general cognitive machinery happens to be able to do, and because it was never optimized, you see enormous variance. A grandmaster and a casual club player are separated by a gap that's hard to even describe. The grandmaster will win essentially every game, forever. That kind of spread is just not something you see in abilities that evolution actually cared about.

Compare that to something like walking, or catching a ball, or recognizing a face. These are things where humans were under intense selection for hundreds of millions of years, going back long before we were human. If you couldn't move through the world competently, you died. So the variation got compressed. Almost everyone is roughly at the same level, and the level is extraordinarily high. We don't appreciate how high because it's universal, but if you try to build a robot that does what a toddler does with its hands, you very quickly discover how hard the problem is.

So I'd frame it as: the variance in a skill tells you something about how long and how hard that skill has been optimized for. Low variance, high floor, means a lot of optimization has already happened. High variance means you're looking at a capability that's essentially an accident of general intelligence. And I think this is actually a useful lens for thinking about AI progress too. The things that look impressive to us, like chess or math or writing code, are often the things that are new and unoptimized for humans, so they're comparatively easy for machines to surpass us at. The things that look trivial, like sensorimotor control, are the ones where evolution has already done an enormous amount of work, and that's where machines have been struggling for decades. It's essentially Moravec's paradox, but I think the variance framing explains why the paradox exists rather than just naming it.

r001.rationale: The response says chess is unoptimized and highly variable, but does not explain that inefficient use of the brain’s computational resources leaves room to improve performance.

r002.rationale: It treats the enormous spread in chess ability as evidence that chess was never optimized by evolution.

r003.rationale: It says humans were never selected for chess and that chess is comparatively easy for machines to surpass us at.

r004.rationale: It says sensorimotor variation was compressed by intense evolutionary selection, leaving most people at a similarly high level.

astra-6.text:
I think a lot of it comes down to what we’ve had evolutionary pressure to be good at. Humans have been doing things like navigating their environment, recognizing objects, and manipulating things for a very long time. So we all come with a lot of machinery that makes those tasks feel almost effortless, even though computationally they’re quite difficult.

Chess is different. We haven’t evolved specifically to play chess. We’re taking more general learning abilities and applying them to this fairly unusual task, and people differ enormously in how much practice they’ve had and how effectively they learn from it. So you get this very wide spread between a beginner and a grandmaster.

But there’s also a measurement issue. We have a very precise way of comparing chess players, whereas we tend to lump everyday sensorimotor abilities together as things that everyone can do. If you look at gymnastics or juggling, you can see substantial differences there too. So I wouldn’t take the apparent contrast as evidence that chess is intrinsically more computationally demanding than perception or movement.

r001.rationale: The response attributes chess variation to practice and learning differences, but does not explain that inefficient cognitive algorithms leave room to improve performance by using the brain’s computational resources more efficiently.

r002.rationale: It says humans have not evolved specifically for chess, but explains the wide spread through differences in practice and measurement rather than interpreting that spread as evidence of poor optimization.

r003.rationale: The response says humans have not evolved specifically to play chess, which explains why computers outperforming humans at chess would be unsurprising.

r004.rationale: The response says evolution gave humans machinery for sensorimotor tasks, but does not interpret their relatively small variation as evidence that evolution substantially optimized those abilities; it instead questions the apparent contrast in variation.

sol-6.1.text:
I think a lot of it comes down to how much optimization has gone into those abilities. Almost everyone gets an enormous amount of practice at moving around, recognizing objects, and interacting with the physical world. And evolution has been selecting for those abilities for a very long time. Chess is a much more unusual activity, where people vary enormously in how much time they’ve spent practicing and studying.

So when we say that one person is vastly better at chess than another, we’re often comparing someone who has devoted a substantial fraction of their life to it with someone who barely knows the rules. We don’t usually make that kind of comparison for walking or recognizing faces.

There’s also the question of how we measure ability. Chess gives you a competitive setting where relatively small differences can translate into one person winning almost every game. Everyday sensorimotor tasks often just look like success or failure: both people pick up the cup. That can hide differences in how precisely or reliably they do it. So I wouldn’t immediately interpret the variation in chess performance as evidence that the underlying cognitive abilities vary much more than sensorimotor abilities.

r001.rationale: The response discusses practice and evolution but does not say cognitive algorithms are poorly optimized or that using the brain’s computational resources more efficiently could improve performance.

r002.rationale: It attributes chess variation largely to differences in practice and study; it does not interpret that variation as evidence that humans are poorly optimized for chess.

r003.rationale: It does not discuss computers outperforming humans at chess or explain that comparison through the lack of evolutionary selection for chess ability.

r004.rationale: It says evolution selected for sensorimotor abilities, but does not interpret their relatively small variation as evidence that evolution substantially optimized them. It instead notes that everyday measures may hide differences.
